disease.scientific_name: Anxiety Disorders / Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD) / Panic Disorder / Social Anxiety Disorder / Specific Phobia / Agoraphobia / Separation Anxiety Disorder

overview.description: Anxiety disorders are a family of related but distinct mental health conditions characterised by excessive, persistent, and often disabling fear, worry, and apprehension — disproportionate to the actual threat presented — accompanied by physical symptoms (palpitations, trembling, sweating, breathlessness, nausea, dizziness) and behavioural changes (particularly AVOIDANCE of anxiety-provoking situations). Anxiety disorders are the most prevalent mental health conditions in the world, affecting an estimated 264 million people globally (WHO 2019) — and the most prevalent of all psychiatric diagnoses in India, where they affect an estimated 45-50 million people. A critical conceptual distinction: NORMAL ANXIETY is a universal and functional human emotion — an adaptive evolutionary response (the 'fight-or-flight' response) that prepares the body to face or flee threats, sharpens focus during examinations or important events, and motivates action; PATHOLOGICAL ANXIETY (anxiety disorder) occurs when this response becomes: disproportionate to the actual threat; persistent without resolution; uncontrollable despite recognising it is excessive; and impairing — significantly disrupting the person's ability to work, study, maintain relationships, or enjoy daily life. Anxiety disorders are distinguished from normal anxiety by DURATION (weeks to months not minutes), INTENSITY (severe, distressing, not proportionate to the situation), PERVASIVENESS (multiple life domains affected), and FUNCTIONAL IMPAIRMENT (work, relationships, physical health significantly disrupted). India faces a distinctive anxiety landscape shaped by factors unique to Indian society: extraordinary academic pressure from highly competitive examinations (JEE, NEET, UPSC, CA Foundation — where the gap between the number of aspirants and available seats creates near-universal examination anxiety among young people); a rapidly changing social fabric where traditional joint family structures are breaking down while new social stressors (social media comparison, urban migration, economic insecurity) are rising; massive cultural stigma against mental illness that drives somatisation (presenting physical symptoms to cardiologists and neurologists rather than seeking psychiatric help — 'my heart is beating fast' rather than 'I am having a panic attack'); a catastrophic shortage of mental health professionals (India has approximately 9,000 psychiatrists and 2,000 clinical psychologists for 1.4 billion people — less than 1 per 100,000 population vs the WHO recommendation of 3 per 100,000); and the widespread inappropriate prescription and self-medication with benzodiazepines (particularly alprazolam — one of the most prescribed drugs in India, often given by general physicians as a 'quick fix' without proper psychiatric evaluation or evidence-based psychotherapy, creating a silent epidemic of benzodiazepine dependence). Anxiety disorders are highly treatable — with first-line evidence-based treatments including specific psychotherapies (Cognitive Behavioural Therapy — CBT, the gold standard), pharmacotherapy (SSRIs/SNRIs as first-line), and lifestyle interventions (exercise, yoga, mindfulness) achieving 60-80% response rates. The tragedy in India is not the lack of effective treatments but the enormous treatment gap: only 10-12% of Indians with anxiety disorders ever receive any form of treatment.
overview.affected_organ: Brain (amygdala — fear centre; prefrontal cortex — executive control and threat appraisal; hippocampus — memory and contextualisation; hypothalamus — HPA axis activation; locus coeruleus — norepinephrine release); Autonomic nervous system (sympathetic activation — fight-or-flight); HPA axis (hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal — chronic cortisol dysregulation); Cardiovascular system (tachycardia, palpitations); Respiratory system (hyperventilation); Gastrointestinal system (nausea, diarrhoea, IBS); Musculoskeletal system (tension, tremor); Sleep architecture (insomnia from hyperarousal)

neurobiology.amygdala: The fear-processing centre of the brain — detects threats and triggers the fear response; in anxiety disorders, the amygdala is hyperactive and hyperreactive — it generates an alarm response even to relatively non-threatening stimuli; the amygdala communicates with the hypothalamus (triggering physical symptoms) and the prefrontal cortex (which normally provides 'top-down' regulation of fear but is dysfunctional in anxiety disorders)
neurobiology.prefrontal_cortex: The rational 'reasoning' part of the brain — normally regulates amygdala activity (telling it 'this is not actually dangerous'); in anxiety disorders, the prefrontal cortex underactivation means the amygdala is 'unregulated', generating persistent fear responses without the normal cognitive override; CBT works by training the prefrontal cortex to better regulate amygdala responses
neurobiology.hpa_axis: Chronic anxiety activates the Hypothalamus-Pituitary-Adrenal axis → sustained cortisol release → impairs immune function; damages hippocampal neurons (memory and contextualisation); worsens cardiovascular risk; perpetuates the anxiety cycle (cortisol itself increases anxiety sensitivity)

neurotransmitters.serotonin: Reduced serotonergic tone in anxiety circuits; SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram) work by increasing synaptic serotonin availability in amygdala and prefrontal circuits — the basis for their anxiolytic efficacy
neurotransmitters.gaba: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain — reduced GABAergic tone in anxiety; benzodiazepines work by potentiating GABA-A receptor activity, producing rapid anxiolysis; buspirone works on 5-HT1A receptors reducing amygdala activity
neurotransmitters.norepinephrine: Locus coeruleus hyperactivity → norepinephrine surge → physical anxiety symptoms (tachycardia, sweating, tremor); SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) reduce both serotonergic and noradrenergic dysfunction in anxiety
neurotransmitters.glutamate: Emerging role of glutamatergic hyperactivity in anxiety circuits; ketamine and mGluR modulators are experimental targets

overview.prevalence: Global: approximately 264 million people (WHO 2019); 12-month prevalence 4.0%; lifetime prevalence 7.3%; most common mental health condition worldwide; India: 4-6% lifetime prevalence; estimated 40-50 million affected; female to male ratio 2:1; NIMHANS National Mental Health Survey (2016): 3.4% of Indian adults have anxiety disorders requiring treatment; only 10-12% ever seek or receive treatment; COVID-19 dramatically increased anxiety prevalence — post-COVID surveys show 15-25% of Indians reporting anxiety symptoms
overview.age_group: All ages; most anxiety disorders begin in childhood or young adulthood (Social Anxiety Disorder median onset 13 years; Specific Phobias 7-11 years; GAD 30s; Panic Disorder late teens to 30s); often goes unrecognised and untreated for years to decades in India
overview.gender: Overall 2:1 female predominance; social anxiety disorder approximately equal; substance-related anxiety presentations more common in males
overview.is_curable_note: Anxiety disorders are highly treatable — 60-80% of patients achieve significant symptom reduction with appropriate treatment (CBT, SSRIs/SNRIs, or both); many achieve full remission; treatment is not about 'curing' anxiety entirely (some anxiety is normal and protective) but about restoring proportionate, controllable anxiety that does not significantly impair daily life; some patients require long-term management particularly for GAD and panic disorder
overview.key_fact: Anxiety disorders are the most common mental health conditions in India — yet fewer than 1 in 10 affected people receive any form of treatment. The combination of massive cultural stigma, acute shortage of mental health professionals, widespread benzodiazepine dependence (prescribed by non-specialist physicians as a quick fix), and somatisation (seeking cardiac and GI care for physical symptoms of anxiety) creates a perfect storm of undertreatment. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) is the gold standard treatment — as effective as medication, with longer-lasting benefits — but is severely under-available in India. Regular aerobic exercise and yoga are scientifically proven to reduce anxiety and should be prescribed alongside other treatments.

types.name: Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD)
types.description: The most common anxiety disorder — characterised by persistent, excessive, and uncontrollable worry about multiple everyday topics (work performance, health, family, finances, minor daily matters) for at least 6 months, accompanied by physical and psychological tension symptoms. The person recognises the worry is excessive and difficult to control but cannot stop it. GAD is sometimes called 'the worrying disease' — the hallmark is GENERALISED worry about multiple things simultaneously, unlike other anxiety disorders that have specific focus (panic attacks in Panic Disorder; social situations in Social Anxiety Disorder).
types.dsm5_criteria: A: Excessive anxiety and worry about multiple events/activities, most days for ≥6 months; B: Difficulty controlling the worry; C: ≥3 of: restlessness/feeling on edge; easily fatigued; difficulty concentrating; irritability; muscle tension; sleep disturbance; D: Clinically significant distress or functional impairment; E: Not due to substances or medical conditions; F: Not better explained by another mental disorder
clinical_features: EXCESSIVE UNCONTROLLABLE WORRY — worrying 'all the time' about multiple things; jumping from one worry to another; worst-case scenario thinking; difficulty tolerating uncertainty ('what if' thinking)
RESTLESSNESS AND FEELING KEYED UP — unable to relax; physical tension; cannot sit still; sense of inner trembling
EASY FATIGABILITY — chronic exhaustion from sustained anxiety; even without vigorous activity
CONCENTRATION DIFFICULTIES — mind 'goes blank'; difficulty making decisions; cannot complete tasks; intrusive worries interfere with concentration
IRRITABILITY — short temper; low frustration tolerance; snapping at family members; related to chronic tension
MUSCLE TENSION — tightness in neck, shoulders, and back; headaches (tension-type); jaw clenching (bruxism); generalised aches
SLEEP DISTURBANCE — difficulty falling asleep (hyperarousal); frequent waking (mind racing at night); unrefreshing sleep; morning fatigue
types.india_presentations: GAD is particularly common in India around: examination anxiety in students (perpetual worry about academic performance); financial anxiety (economic insecurity, job security); health anxiety (frequent health worries; consulting multiple doctors for physical symptoms of anxiety — 'somatisation'); family and marital anxiety (arranged marriage pressures, joint family conflicts, dowry concerns); workplace performance anxiety
types.screening_tool: GAD-7 (Generalised Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale): scores 0-21; Mild 5-9; Moderate 10-14; Severe 15-21; validated in Indian populations
types.management: CBT (evidence-based gold standard — particularly effective for GAD); SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram — first-line pharmacotherapy); SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine); buspirone (non-addictive anxiolytic — for GAD); exercise and yoga; relaxation techniques; mindfulness

types.name: Panic Disorder
types.description: Characterised by recurrent, unexpected PANIC ATTACKS followed by at least 1 month of: persistent concern about having future panic attacks; worry about the implications or consequences of attacks ('I am having a heart attack'; 'I am going mad'; 'I will lose control'); and/or significant maladaptive behavioural changes related to attacks (avoidance). The PANIC ATTACK itself is a discrete episode of intense fear or discomfort peaking within minutes — the most dramatic and terrifying manifestation of anxiety.
types.panic_attack_features: A panic attack involves at least 4 of: palpitations, pounding heart, or accelerated heart rate; sweating; trembling or shaking; shortness of breath or smothering sensation; feelings of choking; chest pain or discomfort; nausea or abdominal distress; dizziness, unsteadiness, light-headedness, or faintness; chills or hot flushes; paraesthesias (numbness or tingling sensations); derealisation (feeling of unreality) or depersonalisation (feeling detached from oneself); fear of losing control or going crazy; fear of dying
types.clinical_pattern: UNEXPECTED (uncued) panic attacks are diagnostic of Panic Disorder — occurring without an obvious trigger, even during sleep (nocturnal panic attacks); EXPECTED (cued) attacks occur reliably in specific situations (heights, social situations — more typical of specific phobia or social anxiety)
types.catastrophic_misinterpretation: The psychological core of panic disorder is CATASTROPHIC MISINTERPRETATION of benign physical sensations — racing heart from walking upstairs is interpreted as 'heart attack'; slight breathlessness as 'suffocating'; dizziness as 'stroke'; this creates a feedback loop (misinterpretation → fear → more physical symptoms → more misinterpretation → full panic attack)
types.india_context: In India, panic attacks are almost universally first misdiagnosed as CARDIAC CONDITIONS — patients present to emergency departments with 'chest pain', 'heart attack', 'palpitations'; undergo extensive cardiac investigations (ECG, echocardiogram, treadmill test, Holter monitor); all results are normal; the diagnosis of panic disorder is often delayed by months to years while patients receive unnecessary investigations and cardiac medications; this cardiac somatisation is very prevalent in India (cultural tendency to somatise distress as heart problems — 'mere dil ki dhadkan bahut badhti hai' — 'my heart beats very fast' rather than 'I am anxious')
types.management: CBT with panic-focused modules (interoceptive exposure — deliberate induction of feared physical sensations in controlled settings to break catastrophic misinterpretation cycle); SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine, escitalopram — first-line); SNRIs; breathing retraining; education about the physiology of panic attacks; controlled diaphragmatic breathing

types.name: Social Anxiety Disorder (Social Phobia)
types.description: Marked fear or anxiety about one or more social situations in which the person is exposed to possible scrutiny by others — fear of acting in a way or showing anxiety symptoms that will be humiliating, embarrassing, or lead to rejection. The feared situations are either avoided or endured with intense anxiety or distress. Duration: typically ≥6 months in adults. Social anxiety disorder is the third most common psychiatric disorder globally (after depression and alcohol use disorder) — and one of the most underdiagnosed in India due to cultural normalisation ('shy' or 'introverted' rather than 'unwell').
types.feared_situations: Performance situations (public speaking — most common; eating in public; writing in front of others; using public toilets — shy bladder syndrome); INTERACTIONAL situations (meetings; parties; initiating conversations; asserting oneself; speaking to authority figures; speaking on phone; interviews; dating)
types.core_cognitions: Excessive negative self-evaluation ('I will say something stupid'); hypervigilance to perceived signs of disapproval; intense focus on own performance rather than conversation; mind-reading ('they think I am boring/anxious/incompetent'); post-event processing ('that was so embarrassing') — replaying social interactions negatively for hours or days afterwards
types.safety_behaviours: The paradoxically maintained anxiety through 'safety behaviours' — things done to prevent feared consequences: over-preparation for any social event; avoiding eye contact; speaking very quietly; standing on the periphery of groups; wearing extra deodorant; sitting near exits; carrying water; rehearsing conversations in advance; these behaviours maintain the anxiety because they prevent disconfirmation of catastrophic beliefs
types.india_relevance: Social anxiety in India is amplified by: ACADEMIC PRESSURE (class presentations, seminars, viva voce examinations); ARRANGED MARRIAGE CONTEXT (meeting prospective partners and families — extremely anxiety-provoking); WORKPLACE HIERARCHY (speaking to seniors or bosses; giving presentations); GENDER ROLES (particularly for women in public speaking contexts where anxiety may be reinforced rather than challenged by societal expectations); CULTURAL COLLECTIVISM (shame and 'log kya kahenge' — 'what will people say' — as intensifying social fear)
types.management: CBT (specifically social skills training, cognitive restructuring, and graduated exposure to feared social situations — the most effective treatment); SSRI (sertraline, escitalopram, paroxetine — FDA-approved); SNRI (venlafaxine); group CBT particularly effective (allows direct practice of social situations); beta-blockers (propranolol) for situational performance anxiety only

types.name: Panic Attacks with Agoraphobia
types.description: Agoraphobia is marked fear or anxiety about two or more of the following situations: using public transportation; being in open spaces (markets, parking lots, bridges); being in enclosed spaces (shops, theatres, cinemas, trains); being in a crowd or queue; being outside of the home alone. The person fears or avoids these situations because of thoughts that escape might be difficult or help unavailable in the event of developing panic-like or embarrassing symptoms. Agoraphobia frequently complicates panic disorder (when repeated panic attacks lead to progressive avoidance of situations where attacks have occurred) but can occur without panic disorder.
types.severity_spectrum: Mild: avoids some specific situations but maintains most activities; Severe: housebound — completely unable to leave home alone; Severe agoraphobia is one of the most disabling anxiety conditions and can lead to complete social isolation
types.india_context: Agoraphobia in India is particularly disabling in contexts of: crowded public transport (local trains, buses — if panic attacks occurred there, complete avoidance of public transport follows); crowded market places (bazaars); pilgrimage sites; weddings and large social gatherings; religious festivals
types.management: Graduated in-vivo exposure (gold standard — systematically and progressively approaching avoided situations from least to most feared); CBT with interoceptive exposure; SSRI/SNRI pharmacotherapy; supported by case manager or family member during initial exposure exercises

types.name: Specific Phobia
types.description: Marked fear or anxiety about a specific object or situation (the phobic stimulus) that is actively avoided or endured with intense distress; the fear is disproportionate to the actual danger; causes significant distress or functional impairment. Specific phobias are the most common of all anxiety disorders (lifetime prevalence 7-10%).

subtypes.examples: Spiders (arachnophobia); snakes (ophidiophobia); dogs (cynophobia); rats; cockroaches; India: snake phobia very common (relevant given India has high venomous snake population); dog phobia prominent given free-roaming dog population in Indian cities

Fear of blood, injections, needles, or medical procedures; unique vasovagal response (blood pressure DROPS rather than rises — fainting common); very prevalent in India — needle phobia affects compliance with vaccinations and blood tests
Aeroplanes; enclosed spaces (claustrophobia — very common); elevators; tunnels; bridges; driving

Vomiting phobia (emetophobia — very common); choking phobia; fear of contamination (often OCD spectrum); fear of specific foods; cosmic/religious fears ('cursed', 'evil eye' — important cultural context in India where fear related to supernatural beliefs can cause significant anxiety)

types.management: Specific phobias respond very well to EXPOSURE THERAPY (graduated or flooding — systematic exposure to the feared stimulus); a single session of 3-hour intensive exposure therapy can achieve lasting remission in many specific phobias; no pharmacotherapy shown consistently effective for specific phobias (though propranolol pre-exposure, D-cycloserine augmentation, and virtual reality exposure are being studied)

types.name: Separation Anxiety Disorder
types.description: Excessive fear or anxiety about separation from attachment figures (parents, caregivers, partners) — beyond what is expected for the person's developmental level; persistent for ≥4 weeks in children and ≥6 months in adults. While most common in children, the DSM-5 now includes adult separation anxiety (previously not formally recognised), which manifests as excessive dependence in adult relationships and anxiety about partners or parents being harmed or absent.
types.childhood_presentation: Recurrent excessive distress when separated or anticipating separation from home or attachment figures; persistent worry about losing or harm coming to attachment figures; refusal to go to school (school refusal); reluctance to be alone at home; recurrent nightmares involving separation themes; physical symptoms (nausea, headache, stomach ache) when separation anticipated
types.india_relevance: School refusal anxiety is a significant problem in Indian schools — with competitive academic environments, fear of bullying, and high-pressure learning environments driving school avoidance; adult separation anxiety is seen in the context of arranged marriages and over-enmeshed family relationships; boarding school anxieties; children of working mothers (particularly in joint families disrupted by nuclear migration)
types.management: Family-based CBT (child + family involved); gradual reintegration to school (school-based support); parent coaching (how to respond to child's separation anxiety without reinforcing it); SSRI if severe (sertraline in children — FDA-approved for OCD in children ≥6 years, used off-label for anxiety)

types.name: Health Anxiety (Illness Anxiety Disorder / Hypochondriasis)
types.description: Preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness — despite medical evaluation showing no or minimal medical pathology; excessive health-related behaviours (seeking repeated reassurance from doctors; checking body for signs of disease; excessive internet health searches) or maladaptive avoidance (avoiding medical care from fear of what might be found). Health anxiety exists on a spectrum from minimal concern to complete disability from fear of disease.
types.india_prevalence: Extremely common in India — the largest cause of 'doctor shopping' (consulting multiple specialists for the same physical complaints); closely related to somatic symptom disorder (the physical expression of anxiety and depression); very prevalent in the context of widespread health misinformation on social media and WhatsApp (forwarded 'health alerts' causing mass anxiety about cancer, heart disease, liver disease); significant healthcare resource utilisation
types.cyber_hypochondria: The internet and especially WhatsApp health forwards create an epidemic of health anxiety — 'cyberchondria' — in India; patients arrive with printed diagnoses from Google symptom searches; managing cyberchondria requires digital health literacy education as part of treatment
types.management: CBT (health-specific modules — exposure to feared health situations; reducing reassurance-seeking; limiting health checking; challenging catastrophic interpretations of bodily sensations); SSRIs; psychoeducation about the mind-body connection; addressing underlying anxiety disorder

severity_levels.name: Mild Anxiety — Subclinical or Minimal Impairment
severity_levels.description: Anxiety symptoms present but not significantly impairing daily functioning; manageable with self-help strategies and lifestyle modifications.
severity_levels.criteria: GAD-7 score 5-9; anxiety present and distressing but daily activities maintained; work/study functioning adequate; relationships maintained; no panic attacks or avoidance behaviours; no suicidal ideation
severity_levels.functional_impact: Mild difficulty relaxing; occasional worry; normal activities maintained; subclinical quality-of-life impairment
severity_levels.management: Psychoeducation (understanding anxiety); self-help CBT workbooks; regular aerobic exercise (30 min 5×/week — proven anxiolytic); yoga and pranayama; sleep hygiene; caffeine reduction; mindfulness apps; brief counselling; reassessment at 4-6 weeks

severity_levels.name: Moderate Anxiety — Significant Impairment
severity_levels.description: Anxiety substantially interfering with work, relationships, or daily activities; requires active treatment.
severity_levels.criteria: GAD-7 score 10-14; significant distress; occupational or academic performance noticeably affected; social withdrawal; avoidance of some situations; possible panic attacks; sleep significantly disrupted; somatic symptoms causing GP visits
severity_levels.functional_impact: Reduced work/academic performance; social withdrawal; avoidance of some previously enjoyed activities; sleep disrupted; physical health impacting
severity_levels.management: CBT by trained therapist (6-12 sessions); SSRI (sertraline or escitalopram first-line — start low, titrate); or CBT + SSRI combined (superior to either alone for moderate severity); yoga; exercise; sleep hygiene; reassessment at 4-8 weeks; suicide risk screening at every visit

severity_levels.name: Severe Anxiety — Major Functional Impairment
severity_levels.description: Anxiety causing major disruption across multiple life domains; significant distress; possible agoraphobia or significant avoidance.
severity_levels.criteria: GAD-7 score 15-21; significant occupational/academic dysfunction (unable to work or study normally); significant social or agoraphobic avoidance; recurrent panic attacks; severe insomnia; significant relationship strain; possible comorbid depression
severity_levels.functional_impact: Unable to perform normal duties; significant social isolation; constant distress; physical health significantly impacted; quality of life severely reduced
severity_levels.management: Psychiatry referral; SSRI at therapeutic dose + CBT; consider augmentation (buspirone add-on; pregabalin for GAD); brief limited benzodiazepine only if extreme distress during initial SSRI titration period (maximum 2-4 weeks); occupational or academic adjustment; family psychoeducation; monthly review

severity_levels.name: Critical — Severe Anxiety with Suicidal Ideation or Complete Disability
severity_levels.description: Anxiety disorder causing complete functional collapse, suicidal ideation, self-harm, or psychiatric emergency.
severity_levels.criteria: Housebound agoraphobia; unable to work, maintain relationships, or perform self-care; suicidal ideation (passive 'I wish I were dead' or active 'I am thinking of harming myself'); anxiety with psychotic features (rare); severe depression with anxiety requiring urgent psychiatric assessment
severity_levels.management: EMERGENCY: immediate psychiatric assessment; crisis helpline activation (iCall: 9152987821; Vandrevala: 1860-2662-345; NIMHANS helpline: 080-46110007; National Mental Health Helpline iMHAS: 14416); hospitalisation consideration; urgent SSRI initiation; structured safety planning; family involvement; NEVER leave the person alone if actively suicidal

causes.aetiology_overview: Anxiety disorders arise from the complex interaction of biological (genetic, neurobiological), psychological (cognitive, behavioral), and social (environmental, cultural, life events) factors — the 'biopsychosocial model'. No single cause creates an anxiety disorder; rather, a vulnerability (biological predisposition + early experiences) interacts with precipitating events (stressors, traumas) and maintaining factors (avoidance, unhelpful thinking patterns) to create the disorder.
risk_factors: GENETIC PREDISPOSITION: anxiety disorders have approximately 30-40% heritability; first-degree relatives of people with anxiety disorders have 2-6× higher risk; specific genetic variants in serotonin transporter gene (5-HTTLPR), COMT, BDNF are implicated; anxiety and depression share substantial genetic architecture

CHILDHOOD ADVERSITY: childhood abuse (physical, sexual, emotional); neglect; parental separation or loss; witnessing domestic violence; parental anxiety or mental illness (modelling anxious behaviour and threat appraisal); overly critical or controlling parenting (reducing child's sense of competence and safety); early bullying; all significantly increase adult anxiety disorder risk

TEMPERAMENT: behavioural inhibition (a tendency in infants and toddlers to withdraw from novel situations, be cautious with strangers, and be physiologically reactive) is the strongest temperamental predictor of childhood and adult anxiety disorders; neuroticism (personality trait of negative affect) confers elevated anxiety risk

TRAUMA AND LIFE EVENTS: recent trauma (road accident, assault, natural disaster, serious illness, bereavement); cumulative stressors; significant life transitions (migration, marriage, job loss, new responsibility); pandemic (COVID-19 dramatically increased anxiety across India)

CHRONIC STRESS: sustained occupational stress; caregiver burden (parents of children with serious illness; adult children of elderly dependent parents); chronic physical illness; financial stress; marital conflict
INDIA-SPECIFIC STRESSORS:

Academic pressure: JEE/NEET/UPSC/Board examination anxiety — affecting millions of Indian students; particularly severe in South India where competitive examination culture is extremely intense; suicide rates among Indian students from examination stress are among the world's highest

Competitive examination culture: the gap between aspirants (millions) and seats (thousands) creates a near-universal experience of high-stakes failure; multiple attempt cycles; family financial investment in coaching creating additional pressure

Social media and comparison: constant comparison with peers; FOMO (fear of missing out); cyberbullying; social media perfectionism culture; WhatsApp group pressure; particularly affecting Indian adolescents and young adults

Workplace anxiety: IT sector high-performance culture; target-driven corporate environments; job insecurity; long working hours; night shifts (call centre workers — circadian disruption worsening anxiety)

Economic anxiety: rapidly rising cost of living; housing costs; job market insecurity; agricultural distress (farmer anxiety — linked to farm loan burden, monsoon uncertainty, market price volatility)
Family and relationship pressures: arranged marriage process; in-law conflicts; dowry pressure; marital discord; pressure to have children; gender role expectations
MEDICAL CONDITIONS CAUSING OR WORSENING ANXIETY — must be excluded:
Hyperthyroidism — nearly identical to GAD; tremor, palpitations, anxiety, heat intolerance; TSH is the first test in any new anxiety disorder
Cardiac arrhythmia (especially SVT) — episodic palpitations; may mimic panic attacks
Phaeochromocytoma (rare) — paroxysmal hypertension, sweating, palpitations, anxiety
Cushing's syndrome — cortisol excess; anxiety and mood disturbance
Hypoglycaemia — episodic anxiety, sweating, trembling; diabetics on insulin particularly
Anaemia — fatigue, palpitations, breathlessness triggering health anxiety

Caffeine excess — very common; strong tea (chai — multiple cups daily in India), coffee, energy drinks; caffeine directly increases anxiety, palpitations, and tremor; a major modifiable factor in Indian patients

SUBSTANCE-RELATED: alcohol (initial relief but rebound anxiety worsening; withdrawal causes severe anxiety and panic); stimulants (cocaine, amphetamines, ecstasy); cannabis (paradoxically increases anxiety in some users — high-THC cannabis is a common precipitant of panic attacks and paranoid anxiety in young Indians); benzodiazepine withdrawal (common in India given widespread BZD use — withdrawal causes severe anxiety, panic, and seizures)

MEDICATIONS CAUSING ANXIETY: steroids (high-dose prednisolone causes anxiety, mania); bronchodilators (salbutamol — tremor and tachycardia mimicking anxiety); decongestants (pseudoephedrine); some thyroid supplements; methylphenidate; antihistamines (paradoxical reaction in some)

symptoms.overview: Anxiety disorder symptoms span three interacting domains — COGNITIVE (thought patterns), PHYSICAL (body sensations), and BEHAVIOURAL (actions and avoidance). Understanding this three-domain model is central to CBT treatment: each domain reinforces the others in a vicious cycle (anxious thoughts → physical symptoms → avoidance → more anxiety → more thoughts). India-specific presentations frequently emphasise SOMATIC (physical) symptoms — chest tightness, palpitations, headaches, GI symptoms, fatigue — rather than the psychological experience of worry or fear, due to cultural patterns of expressing emotional distress through the body (somatisation). This means many Indian anxiety disorder patients first present to cardiologists, neurologists, gastroenterologists, and general physicians rather than psychiatrists.

primary_symptoms.name: Excessive Worry and Apprehension — The Cognitive Core
primary_symptoms.description: Persistent, intrusive, and uncontrollable worry about multiple everyday topics — the defining cognitive symptom of GAD; and in other anxiety disorders, the specific feared topic (social humiliation, health, contamination, separation). WORRY involves repeated mental rehearsal of potential future negative events; it is ego-dystonic (the person recognises it is excessive but cannot stop); it is exhausting, time-consuming (patients often report spending 3-5+ hours per day worrying), and impairs concentration on the present moment. COGNITIVE DISTORTIONS characterising anxiety include: CATASTROPHISING ('if I make a mistake in the presentation, my career is over'); PROBABILITY OVERESTIMATION ('I am probably seriously ill' despite no medical evidence); INTOLERANCE OF UNCERTAINTY ('I cannot stand not knowing what will happen'); MENTAL FILTERING (attending only to threat-relevant information and ignoring disconfirmatory evidence).
primary_symptoms.india_note: In India, worry content frequently focuses on: children's academic performance; family members' health; financial security; social judgment ('log kya kahenge' — excessive worry about others' opinions); future of arranged marriage; job performance

primary_symptoms.name: Physical (Somatic) Symptoms of Anxiety — The Body's Fear Response
primary_symptoms.description: The autonomic nervous system's sympathetic activation during anxiety produces a comprehensive physical response affecting every organ system. These physical symptoms are REAL, distressing, and often severe — not 'imagined' or 'faked'. They are produced by the release of adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline from the adrenal glands and locus coeruleus, triggering the physiological 'fight-or-flight' response. CARDIOVASCULAR: palpitations (awareness of heartbeat); tachycardia (racing heart); chest tightness or discomfort; blood pressure elevation; RESPIRATORY: breathlessness; feeling of smothering; hyperventilation (rapid shallow breathing → CO2 drop → respiratory alkalosis → tingling in hands and face, dizziness, feeling of unreality — which worsens panic); NEUROLOGICAL: dizziness; light-headedness; headache (tension); tingling in extremities and face (from hyperventilation); GASTROINTESTINAL: nausea; 'butterflies in the stomach'; diarrhoea or loose stools; urgency; IBS symptoms; dry mouth; MUSCULOSKELETAL: muscle tension; shoulder and neck stiffness; trembling; jaw clenching; SKIN: sweating; flushing; pallor; GENITOURINARY: frequent urination; sexual dysfunction.
primary_symptoms.india_specific_presentations: Physical symptoms drive most Indian anxiety patients to seek medical care — palpitations to cardiologist; breathlessness to pulmonologist; GI symptoms to gastroenterologist; headaches to neurologist; dizziness to ENT; fatigue and weakness to general physician; each specialist performs appropriate investigations (normal results); patient is frustrated and not improving; the anxiety disorder goes undiagnosed through these multiple specialist consultations; the average time to diagnosis of anxiety disorder in India is 5-10 years from symptom onset

primary_symptoms.name: Avoidance Behaviour — The Behavioural Consequence
primary_symptoms.description: AVOIDANCE is the central behavioural symptom of anxiety disorders — and the single most important MAINTAINING FACTOR that prevents natural recovery. Avoidance provides immediate relief (the anxiety temporarily decreases when the feared situation is avoided) which is powerfully reinforcing (negative reinforcement); but in the long-term, avoidance: prevents the person from learning that the feared situation is safe (no new learning occurs); sensitises the amygdala further (each avoidance strengthens the fear association); progressively restricts the person's life. The clinical definition of an anxiety DISORDER (vs normal anxiety) crucially involves avoidance that significantly impairs life. BEHAVIOURAL AVOIDANCE SPECTRUM: Overt avoidance — not going to a party (social anxiety); not boarding an airplane (specific phobia); not opening a doctor's letter (health anxiety); SUBTLE AVOIDANCE — distraction (using phone during a feared social interaction); escape behaviours (leaving a crowded shop quickly); safety objects (carrying medication 'just in case' that is never taken); COGNITIVE AVOIDANCE — thought suppression; reassurance-seeking; compulsive checking (OCD spectrum); excessive planning and preparation
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild (avoiding a few situations) to Severe (complete housebound agoraphobia)
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: The goal of CBT for anxiety is NOT to reduce anxiety (which is often not possible or even desirable) but to reduce AVOIDANCE — allowing the person to engage with feared situations and discover they are safe or manageable

primary_symptoms.name: Panic Attack — Acute Crescendo Episode
primary_symptoms.description: A sudden surge of intense fear or intense discomfort that reaches a peak within minutes and includes ≥4 physical and cognitive symptoms (see Panic Disorder type for full list). Panic attacks are the most dramatic and medically alarming acute anxiety presentation — patients frequently call ambulances or present to emergency departments believing they are having a heart attack or stroke. Key distinguishing features from cardiac events: panic attacks peak within 10 minutes and typically fully resolve within 20-30 minutes (cardiac events are generally sustained); panic attacks leave no cardiac enzyme elevation, no ECG changes, no haemodynamic instability (though BP and HR transiently rise); panic attacks often occur in specific contexts or predictable patterns (though can be nocturnal); full recovery between attacks.
primary_symptoms.severity: Severe (acutely — though not medically dangerous in healthy individuals)
primary_symptoms.india_emergency: Panic attack patients in India frequently arrive by ambulance to cardiac emergency departments; cost of unnecessary investigations per undiagnosed panic disorder patient (average 5-10 years to correct diagnosis) estimated Rs 50,000-200,000 in unnecessary cardiac workup

primary_symptoms.name: Sleep Disturbance from Anxiety
primary_symptoms.description: Insomnia is near-universal in anxiety disorders — arising from HYPERAROUSAL (the anxious nervous system cannot downregulate sufficiently for sleep onset) and NOCTURNAL WORRY (mind racing at night without the distractions of daytime). SLEEP INITIATION INSOMNIA (difficulty falling asleep): lying awake with racing thoughts; typically takes 1-3 hours to fall asleep; SLEEP MAINTENANCE INSOMNIA (waking during the night): waking at 2-4 AM with flood of worries; unable to return to sleep; EARLY MORNING AWAKENING (less typical for anxiety, more typical for depression — though overlap is common). Sleep deprivation from anxiety worsens anxiety the following day (sleep-deprived amygdala is 60% more reactive to threat stimuli) — creating a vicious cycle. NOCTURNAL PANIC ATTACKS: waking suddenly from sleep in full panic (no precipitating nightmare) — characteristic of panic disorder.

secondary_symptoms: Irritability and low frustration tolerance — from chronic tension and sleep deprivation; snapping at family; short fuse; interpersonal relationship strain
Fatigue and exhaustion — sustained anxiety is physiologically exhausting; chronic cortisol elevation depletes energy reserves; comorbid depression amplifies fatigue
Difficulty concentrating and brain fog — anxiety impairs working memory and executive function (prefrontal cortex hypoactivation); difficulty at work or school; mind going blank

Depersonalisation and derealisation — feeling detached from oneself (watching oneself from outside) or the environment feeling unreal ('dream-like'); particularly in panic disorder and severe anxiety; very frightening when first experienced; completely reversible with anxiety treatment
Trembling and shakiness — fine tremor from adrenaline release; hands shake when nervous; voice trembles in social anxiety; tremor worsened by caffeine

Excessive sweating (diaphoresis) — palmar sweating; hyperhidrosis from anxiety; particularly prominent in social anxiety (fear of visible sweating causing further social embarrassment — a particularly painful feedback loop)

Hair loss (alopecia) — chronic stress and anxiety-related cortisol elevation can cause telogen effluvium (diffuse hair shedding); extremely distressing for Indian women for whom hair health is culturally significant; addressing the underlying anxiety resolves the hair loss

Sexual dysfunction — reduced libido; erectile dysfunction in men; arousal difficulties in women; from chronic sympathetic dominance (sympathetic activation is antagonistic to sexual function, which requires parasympathetic dominance); a frequently unasked and undisclosed symptom requiring sensitive enquiry

Skin conditions worsened by anxiety — acne; eczema; psoriasis (anxiety triggers and maintains all three through cortisol and inflammatory pathways); common presenting complaint particularly in urban Indian young adults

somatisation_in_india.description: Somatisation — the expression of psychological distress through physical symptoms — is the dominant presentation pattern for anxiety disorders in India. Multiple cultural, social, and linguistic factors drive somatisation: mental illness stigma (reporting a physical symptom is more socially acceptable than admitting to anxiety or stress); limited psychological vocabulary in many Indian languages to precisely describe internal emotional states; cultural idioms of distress (e.g., 'thinking too much' — sochta rehta hai — as a descriptor for anxiety; 'brain heating' — dimag garam hona — for tension; 'heart burning' — kalejey mein jalan — for grief/worry); the biomedical model reinforced by family ('go see a doctor and get some medicine' vs 'talk to someone about your feelings')
common_somatic_presentations: CARDIAC: palpitations; chest pain; 'heart weakness' (dil ki kamzori) — very common Indian idiom for anxiety/depression; patients consult cardiologists for years before psychiatric diagnosis
NEUROLOGICAL: headaches (tension-type); dizziness; tingling; weakness; 'nerve weakness' (naso ki kamzori) — consult neurologists; MRI brain ordered unnecessarily
GASTROINTESTINAL: IBS symptoms; nausea; chronic abdominal pain; loss of appetite; acid reflux — consult gastroenterologists
MUSCULOSKELETAL: back pain; neck pain; joint pain; generalised aches; consult orthopaedics and rheumatology
FATIGUE AND WEAKNESS: general weakness (kamzori); fatigue attributed to 'low blood pressure', 'low Vitamin D', 'anaemia' before anxiety is considered
SEXUAL HEALTH: semen 'dhatu' loss anxiety (dhat syndrome — anxiety about seminal discharge causing weakness and illness — a culturally specific anxiety disorder particularly in young Indian men)

medical_history: PRESENTING COMPLAINTS — in detail: what exactly is bothering the patient; duration; triggers (situational, spontaneous); course (constant, episodic, worsening); impact on daily life (work, study, relationships, sleep); previous similar episodes
COGNITIVE SYMPTOMS — do they worry excessively? About what topics? Is it controllable? How many hours per day? Catastrophic thinking? Difficulty concentrating?
PHYSICAL SYMPTOMS — palpitations; breathlessness; dizziness; trembling; sweating; chest tightness; GI symptoms; headaches; sleep disturbance — detailed characterisation
BEHAVIOURAL IMPACT — what do they avoid? What has changed in their activity level and social participation? Safety behaviours?
PANIC ATTACKS — if present: when did first panic attack occur? Frequency? Predictors or spontaneous? What happens during an attack? Duration? What do they do afterwards?
ANXIETY TRIGGERS — situational (specific places, social situations, health-related, separation-related) or generalised (all topics)
MOOD — concurrent depressive symptoms (low mood, anhedonia, hopelessness, guilt) — comorbid depression present in 50-60% of anxiety disorder patients

SUICIDAL IDEATION — ALWAYS ASK; anxiety disorders significantly increase suicide risk particularly when comorbid with depression; passive ideation ('I wish I could escape all this') vs active ideation ('I am thinking of harming myself'); plan; intent; access to means
PAST PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY — prior episodes of anxiety or depression; prior treatment (what, for how long, response); hospitalisations; self-harm history
FAMILY HISTORY — anxiety, depression, OCD, substance use in first-degree relatives

SUBSTANCE USE — alcohol (quantity, frequency, last drink — withdrawal worsens anxiety); caffeine (number of cups of chai/coffee per day — important modifiable factor); cannabis; tobacco (nicotine — paradoxically worsens anxiety despite perceived relief); other substances

MEDICATIONS — current prescriptions; OTC (including herbal medications — some have stimulant effects); over-the-counter cough syrups (codeine-containing — common in India for recreational use); steroid injections

MEDICAL HISTORY — thyroid disease (hyperthyroidism mimics anxiety); cardiac conditions; pheochromocytoma; previous ECG/thyroid test results; any physical illnesses that could be causing or worsening anxiety

SOCIAL HISTORY — occupation (IT sector? Student? Farmer?); relationship status; living situation (joint family?); financial situation; support system (who is supportive?); cultural and religious beliefs (particularly relevant in India — religious beliefs can be protective OR can be a source of anxiety — religious OCD is common); recent life events (marriage, divorce, bereavement, job loss, migration)
CHILDHOOD HISTORY — early experiences of anxiety; parental relationships; traumatic events; school difficulties; early signs of temperamental inhibition
EXAMINATION ANXIETY SPECIFICALLY — for students: which examination? How many attempts? Family pressure? Academic performance to date?
physical_examination: General appearance — anxious appearance; tremor visible at rest or with outstretched hands; sweating; pallor; tachycardia (pulse rate); blood pressure (may be elevated in acute anxiety; consistently elevated warrants investigation for hypertension or phaeochromocytoma)
Thyroid examination — thyroid gland size (goitre suggests thyroid disease); tremor; warm moist skin; exophthalmos (hyperthyroidism — very important to exclude)
Cardiovascular examination — heart rate; rhythm (arrhythmia?); heart sounds; any murmurs; blood pressure bilateral
Neurological examination — exclude primary neurological causes of anxiety-like symptoms (tremor, dizziness); note that most anxiety disorder patients have a completely normal neurological examination
Mental state examination — the psychiatric examination:
APPEARANCE AND BEHAVIOUR: eye contact; psychomotor agitation (restlessness, fidgeting) or retardation; tearfulness; tremor
SPEECH: rate (pressured or slowed); volume; coherence
MOOD: subjective (how patient describes their mood); objective (how the interviewer perceives it)
AFFECT: range (full/restricted); appropriateness to content; reactivity
THOUGHT FORM: logical and goal-directed vs tangential/circumstantial; thought blocking
THOUGHT CONTENT: worries (topics, intensity, controllability); phobias; obsessions; paranoid ideation; suicidal ideation or self-harm thoughts; homicidal ideation
PERCEPTIONS: auditory or visual hallucinations (absent in anxiety disorders — presence suggests psychosis)
COGNITION: orientation; concentration; memory — cognitive testing if cognitive complaints prominent
INSIGHT: does the patient understand they have a mental health condition requiring treatment? Insight is generally INTACT in anxiety disorders (contrasting with psychosis)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: GAD-7 (Generalised Anxiety Disorder 7-Item Scale) — Validated Screening Tool
diagnostic_tests.description: The most widely used and validated brief screening and severity assessment tool for GAD — and also sensitive for other anxiety disorders. Seven items each scored 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day) over the past 2 weeks; total 0-21. Developed by Spitzer et al. (2006); validated in Indian populations (Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, and other regional language translations available). Simple to administer; takes 2-3 minutes; can be completed in the waiting room.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for GAD; assess severity; monitor treatment response (repeat at each visit)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: 0-4: minimal anxiety; 5-9: mild anxiety; 10-14: moderate anxiety; 15-21: severe anxiety; score ≥10 = probably GAD; score ≥8 = probably any anxiety disorder; specific to GAD but sensitive for all anxiety disorders; widely used in Indian primary care and psychiatry settings

diagnostic_tests.description: Four items (2 anxiety + 2 depression) providing a rapid screen for both conditions — ideal for busy primary care settings in India where time is limited. The 2 anxiety items (derived from GAD-7) and 2 depression items (from PHQ-9) identify patients needing further evaluation.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Ultra-brief screening for both anxiety and depression in primary care; not diagnostic — positive screen requires further clinical assessment
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Each item 0-3; total 0-12; anxiety subscale (items 1-2) ≥3 = probable anxiety disorder; depression subscale (items 3-4) ≥3 = probable depression

diagnostic_tests.description: 14-item questionnaire — 7 items each for anxiety and depression; designed to exclude somatic symptoms that might be confounded by physical illness; widely used in general hospital and primary care settings; validated in India.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for anxiety and depression in medically ill patients (where somatic items would be confounded by physical illness); anxiety subscale specifically targets cognitive worry rather than physical symptoms
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Subscale scores 0-21; 0-7: normal; 8-10: borderline; 11-21: probable case

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Thyroid Function Tests — TSH, fT4, fT3
diagnostic_tests.description: MANDATORY first-line investigation for ALL new anxiety presentations — hyperthyroidism (elevated fT4, suppressed TSH) causes tremor, palpitations, anxiety, irritability, weight loss, heat intolerance, and sleep disturbance — a near-perfect mimic of generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder. India has high rates of thyroid disease (10% of women have subclinical thyroid abnormalities; overt hyperthyroidism 1.6% of women). Hypothyroidism can also cause anxiety through associated depression.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude hyperthyroidism as primary or contributing cause of anxiety; mandated before any psychiatric medication is started
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: TSH: normal 0.4-4.0 mIU/L; suppressed TSH + elevated fT4 = hyperthyroidism → refer endocrinology; elevated TSH + low fT4 = hypothyroidism → thyroid hormone replacement
diagnostic_tests.india_note: India has high iodine deficiency in some regions (despite iodised salt) and high Hashimoto's prevalence — thyroid diseases are extremely common and frequently present as anxiety or mood disorders before the metabolic diagnosis is made

diagnostic_tests.description: Anaemia (common in Indian women from dietary iron deficiency and menorrhagia) causes: fatigue; palpitations; breathlessness; dizziness — all of which can be misinterpreted as anxiety symptoms or can worsen underlying anxiety. Correction of anaemia is essential before adequately treating anxiety.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude anaemia as cause of palpitations, breathlessness, and fatigue; screen for concurrent nutritional deficiency

diagnostic_tests.description: Hypoglycaemia in diabetics on insulin or sulfonylureas causes acute episodic anxiety, sweating, trembling, palpitations — mimicking panic attacks. Diabetes itself increases anxiety disorder risk 2-3× (bidirectional relationship). HbA1c screens for undiagnosed diabetes (which may be presenting with anxiety-like hypoglycaemic episodes).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude hypoglycaemia as a cause of episodic anxiety/panic-like symptoms; screen for undiagnosed diabetes

diagnostic_tests.description: Indicated when: palpitations are the dominant presenting symptom; panic attacks are suspected but cardiac arrhythmia needs to be excluded; any cardiac symptoms in patients over 40 years. Important findings to exclude: SVT (supraventricular tachycardia — episodic palpitations, dizziness — can mimic or trigger panic attacks); WPW syndrome (short PR, delta wave — associated with SVT); QT prolongation (relevant before starting psychotropic medications).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude cardiac arrhythmia as cause of palpitations and episodic anxiety-like symptoms; baseline QT before starting psychotropic medications (particularly when tricyclics or antipsychotics are being considered)

diagnostic_tests.description: Consider when: substance use is suspected but denied; anxiety onset is unexplained; particularly relevant in young adults where cannabis, stimulant, or benzodiazepine withdrawal anxiety needs to be excluded. Cannabis is a particularly important anxiety-precipitant in young Indian adults — high-THC cannabis (increasingly available in India) causes acute anxiety and paranoia, and chronic use causes an anxiety disorder.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect substance use as cause of anxiety; particularly cannabis (THC), cocaine, amphetamines, and benzodiazepine use

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Serum Cortisol and 24-hour Urine Cortisol (if Cushing's Suspected)
diagnostic_tests.description: If features of Cushing's syndrome present (central obesity, stretch marks, facial rounding, diabetes, hypertension alongside anxiety) — serum cortisol and 24-hour urinary free cortisol. Cushing's is a rare but important medical cause of anxiety and mood disorders.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude Cushing's syndrome in appropriate clinical context

diagnostic_tests.description: If memory, concentration, or cognitive complaints are significant alongside anxiety — formal neuropsychological testing or brief cognitive screening (MMSE, MoCA) to quantify cognitive dysfunction and exclude primary cognitive disorder (early dementia, ADHD).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Quantify anxiety-related cognitive impairment; distinguish from primary cognitive disorder; ADHD comorbidity assessment (ADHD and anxiety disorders frequently coexist)

medicines.note: Pharmacotherapy for anxiety disorders should be viewed as ONE COMPONENT of a comprehensive treatment plan — not the sole intervention. Evidence consistently shows that COMBINED treatment (medication + CBT) is more effective than either alone, particularly for moderate-severe anxiety. The most critical prescribing principle for India: BENZODIAZEPINES (alprazolam, diazepam, clonazepam) should NOT be prescribed as first-line or long-term treatment for anxiety disorders — they create physical dependence within weeks, do not address the underlying disorder, and often worsen anxiety long-term through rebound effects. Yet they are dramatically overprescribed in India, including by primary care physicians and even psychiatrists. This is the single most important prescribing quality improvement issue in Indian mental health practice. SSRIs and SNRIs are the evidence-based first-line pharmacotherapy. Medications work by reducing the biological substrate of anxiety (normalising serotonergic, noradrenergic, and GABAergic function) — they do not teach coping skills or change thinking patterns, which is why psychotherapy remains essential.
treatment_principles: 1. SSRIs and SNRIs are FIRST-LINE pharmacotherapy for all anxiety disorders — start low (to minimise initial anxiety increase from serotonin activation), go slow (titrate over 2-4 weeks), and allow 6-12 weeks for full therapeutic effect

2. NEVER prescribe benzodiazepines as first-line or long-term treatment for anxiety disorders — physical dependence within 2-4 weeks; rebound anxiety on discontinuation worsens the disorder; tolerance develops rapidly; cognitive impairment; withdrawal seizures risk

3. INFORM PATIENTS that SSRIs may TEMPORARILY INCREASE anxiety in the first 1-2 weeks of treatment (serotonin syndrome side effects — nervousness, insomnia, GI symptoms) before the anxiolytic effect develops at 4-8 weeks; failure to warn leads to early discontinuation

4. MINIMUM TREATMENT DURATION: 12 months after achieving symptom remission before attempting discontinuation; premature discontinuation leads to very high relapse rates; GAD and panic disorder often require longer treatment

5. PSYCHOTHERAPY (CBT) should be offered to ALL anxiety disorder patients — as the primary treatment for mild-moderate anxiety; as combination treatment for severe anxiety; for relapse prevention after medication discontinuation

6. YOGA AND EXERCISE should be prescribed as adjunctive treatments — both have level 1 RCT evidence for anxiety reduction; 30 minutes of aerobic exercise 5 days per week is as effective as medication for mild anxiety

categories.category_name: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) — First-Line Pharmacotherapy
categories.purpose: First-line pharmacological treatment for all anxiety disorders; increase synaptic serotonin availability in anxiety circuits; require 4-12 weeks for full anxiolytic effect; non-addictive; safe for long-term use.
categories.india_note: SSRIs are dramatically underprescribed in India for anxiety (compared to benzodiazepines which are overprescribed); generic versions of all SSRIs are available at low cost in India (Rs 5-30 per tablet); prescribing inertia from GPs who reach for alprazolam as the 'easier' option must be overcome through education

medicines.name: Sertraline — Most Evidence for Broadest Range of Anxiety Disorders

dosage.gad_and_panic: Start 25-50 mg once daily in the morning (with food); increase to 50 mg after 1 week; therapeutic dose for anxiety: 50-100 mg/day; maximum 200 mg/day for OCD
dosage.social_anxiety: 50-100 mg/day; may require higher doses (150-200 mg) for full social anxiety disorder response
dosage.panic_disorder: Start 25 mg (lower starting dose — panic patients particularly sensitive to initial activating effects); increase gradually to 50-150 mg/day
dosage.india_dosing_principle: START LOWER THAN FOR DEPRESSION — anxiety patients are exquisitely sensitive to initial activating side effects; starting at 25 mg reduces early dropout

medicines.mechanism: Blocks serotonin reuptake transporter (SERT) → increases synaptic serotonin in amygdala, prefrontal cortex, and limbic circuits → normalises fear circuit activity over weeks; also increases brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) promoting neuroplasticity in anxiety circuits
medicines.anxiolytic_timeline: Initial effect: mild reduction in physical anxiety symptoms within 2-4 weeks; Full anxiolytic effect: 6-12 weeks; patients must be counselled to persist through the first 2 weeks (which may feel worse before better)
side_effects: Initial activation (first 1-2 weeks): increased anxiety, jitteriness, insomnia, GI upset — resolves spontaneously; WARN PATIENTS in advance
GI disturbance (nausea, diarrhoea) — take with food; often resolves within 2 weeks

Sexual dysfunction (delayed ejaculation in men; reduced libido) — most common reason for non-adherence in young Indian patients; important to ask about specifically; can switch to bupropion add-on or mirtazapine if problematic
Serotonin syndrome (rare — with concurrent triptans, MAOIs, tramadol)
medicines.duration: Minimum 12 months after achieving remission; many patients with recurrent anxiety disorders benefit from longer-term treatment; discuss maintenance vs discontinuation at 12-month review
medicines.approved_for: GAD, Panic Disorder, Social Anxiety Disorder, OCD, PTSD, PMDD

medicines.name: Escitalopram — Well-Tolerated, Highly Selective
medicines.dosage: Start 5-10 mg once daily (with food, in morning); therapeutic dose: 10-20 mg/day; lower starting dose than sertraline due to higher potency
medicines.use_case: First-line for GAD and panic disorder; particularly well-tolerated (fewest drug interactions; good tolerability profile); highly selective SSRI with minimal off-target effects; preferred when tolerability is a priority
medicines.approved_for: GAD, Major Depression (FDA); used widely for all anxiety disorders in clinical practice

medicines.name: Fluoxetine (Prozac) — Longest Half-Life; Forgiving of Missed Doses
medicines.dosage: 10-20 mg once daily (morning — most activating SSRI; do not take at night); therapeutic dose 20-40 mg for anxiety; maximum 60-80 mg for OCD
medicines.use_case: OCD (highest evidence); Panic Disorder; PMDD; Social Anxiety Disorder; the long half-life (7 days for active metabolite norfluoxetine) makes it forgiving of missed doses and reduces discontinuation syndrome
medicines.important_interactions: Most drug interactions of all SSRIs (potent CYP2D6 inhibitor); check interactions with any polypharmacy
medicines.approved_for: Major Depression, OCD, Panic Disorder, Bulimia Nervosa, PMDD

medicines.name: Paroxetine — Most Potent for Panic and Social Anxiety
medicines.dosage: 10 mg once daily starting dose; therapeutic dose: 20-40 mg/day for panic and social anxiety; 40-60 mg for OCD
medicines.use_case: Panic Disorder, Social Anxiety Disorder, GAD, PTSD, OCD — FDA-approved for all; most potent for panic reduction; most sedating SSRI (useful for insomnia component of anxiety — take at night); anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention in elderly)
medicines.caution: MOST SEVERE DISCONTINUATION SYNDROME of all SSRIs — very short half-life; NEVER stop abruptly; taper very slowly over months; patients must be warned strongly; the most common SSRI for discontinuation-related difficulties in India
medicines.approved_for: MDD, OCD, Panic Disorder, Social Anxiety Disorder, GAD, PTSD, PMDD

medicines.name: Fluvoxamine — Preferred for OCD; Unique Sigma Receptor Activity
medicines.dosage: Start 50 mg at bedtime (sedating); therapeutic dose for OCD: 150-300 mg/day in divided doses; anxiety: 100-150 mg/day
medicines.use_case: OCD (first-line alongside fluoxetine); social anxiety disorder; unique sigma-1 receptor agonism may provide additional neuroplastic and anti-inflammatory benefits beyond serotonin reuptake blockade
medicines.approved_for: OCD; used off-label for social anxiety, panic, GAD

categories.purpose: Dual mechanism (serotonin + norepinephrine reuptake inhibition) — comparable efficacy to SSRIs for anxiety disorders; may have superior efficacy for somatic and painful symptoms of anxiety (due to noradrenergic mechanism reducing musculoskeletal pain and tension); particularly useful when anxiety is accompanied by depression.

medicines.name: Venlafaxine Extended-Release (Effexor XR) — Most Evidence Among SNRIs for Anxiety
medicines.dosage: Start 37.5 mg once daily for 7 days; then 75 mg once daily; therapeutic dose for GAD: 75-150 mg/day; panic disorder: 75-225 mg/day; maximum 225 mg/day
medicines.use_case: GAD (FDA-approved — extensive evidence); Panic Disorder (FDA-approved); Social Anxiety Disorder (FDA-approved); combined anxiety and depression; when SSRIs have failed or caused intolerable side effects
side_effects: Blood pressure elevation (dose-dependent — monitor BP, particularly at doses >150 mg)
Discontinuation syndrome (severe if abruptly stopped — particularly vomiting, electric shock sensations — 'brain zaps'; taper over weeks to months)
Cardiac monitoring recommended in higher doses
medicines.approved_for: GAD, Panic Disorder, Social Anxiety Disorder, MDD

medicines.name: Duloxetine — For Anxiety with Somatic Symptoms and Pain
medicines.dosage: Start 30 mg once daily for 2 weeks; then 60 mg/day; maximum 120 mg/day
medicines.use_case: GAD (FDA-approved — particularly effective when somatic anxiety symptoms are prominent: muscle tension, headache, chronic pain); combined anxiety and depression; anxiety with fibromyalgia or chronic pain; anxiety with diabetic neuropathy (multiple uses in a single drug)
medicines.side_effects: Nausea (most common); insomnia or fatigue; blood pressure elevation; discontinuation syndrome
medicines.approved_for: GAD, MDD, Fibromyalgia, Diabetic Neuropathy, Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain

categories.purpose: A unique non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic — specifically for GAD; works via 5-HT1A receptor partial agonism reducing amygdala reactivity; no abuse potential; no sedation; no dependence. Particularly valuable in India for primary care prescribing where benzodiazepine dependence is a major concern.

medicines.name: Buspirone
medicines.dosage: Start 5 mg three times daily; increase to 10-15 mg three times daily over 2-3 weeks; maximum 60 mg/day in divided doses; take consistently (not as needed)
medicines.mechanism: Selective serotonin 5-HT1A receptor partial agonist; reduces amygdala reactivity; also weak dopamine D2 receptor effects; NO activity at GABA receptor (does not cause sedation or dependence)
medicines.advantages: No abuse potential or dependence; no sedation; no cognitive impairment; no withdrawal syndrome; can be used long-term without dependence concerns; IDEAL for patients with history of benzodiazepine dependence
medicines.disadvantages: Slow onset (2-4 weeks for anxiolytic effect — unlike benzodiazepines which work within 30 minutes); requires consistent dosing (not PRN); ineffective in patients previously using benzodiazepines (cross-tolerance reduces efficacy); less effective for panic disorder; less effective than SSRIs overall
medicines.india_significance: Buspirone is significantly underused in India despite being an ideal non-addictive alternative to alprazolam for GAD; ideally suited for primary care use; generic formulations available at Rs 5-15 per tablet

categories.category_name: Benzodiazepines — Short-Term Only; High Dependence Risk — Use with Extreme Caution
categories.purpose: GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulators providing rapid anxiolysis and sedation; role in anxiety disorders is extremely limited; should be prescribed ONLY for specific short-term indications with clear plans for discontinuation.
categories.critical_warning: BENZODIAZEPINES ARE THE MOST OVERPRESCRIBED AND MOST HARMFUL CLASS OF DRUGS FOR ANXIETY IN INDIA: physical dependence develops within 2-4 weeks; cognitive impairment; fall risk in elderly; respiratory depression with alcohol; rebound anxiety on discontinuation (often more severe than original anxiety — perpetuating the cycle); withdrawal syndrome (anxiety, insomnia, seizures — potentially life-threatening) on abrupt discontinuation; tolerance develops — requiring increasing doses for the same effect; do NOT improve the underlying anxiety disorder and may worsen long-term outcomes; THE FIRST PRESCRIPTION OF A BENZODIAZEPINE SHOULD ALWAYS COME WITH A CLEAR PLAN FOR DISCONTINUATION. India is in the midst of a silent benzodiazepine crisis — alprazolam is one of the most prescribed drugs in the entire country.
legitimate_limited_indications: Bridge treatment (maximum 2-4 weeks) while waiting for SSRI to take effect in severe acute anxiety or panic disorder
Procedural anxiety (dental, medical procedures — single dose)
Alcohol withdrawal (diazepam chlordiazepoxide are treatment of choice)

medicines.name: Alprazolam — Most Widely Misused BZD in India
medicines.dosage: 0.25-0.5 mg twice-three times daily for SHORT-TERM ONLY (maximum 2-4 weeks); NEVER increase dose
medicines.critical_india_note: Alprazolam is dramatically overprescribed in India for all forms of anxiety, insomnia, and distress — often by general physicians, cardiologists, and even traditional practitioners without psychiatric evaluation; many patients are maintained on alprazolam for years or decades; alprazolam has the shortest half-life of common BZDs — most severe discontinuation syndrome; creating widespread unrecognised BZD dependence across India; the situation is a major public health crisis that receives inadequate attention

medicines.name: Clonazepam
medicines.dosage: 0.25-0.5 mg twice daily for short-term adjunct
medicines.use_case: Longer half-life than alprazolam — smoother effect; preferred for benzodiazepine tapering/switching when discontinuing alprazolam (switching from short-acting to longer-acting BZD facilitates smoother taper)
medicines.note: Also used as anticonvulsant (epilepsy — where long-term use is indicated)

medicines.name: Diazepam
medicines.form: Tablet (2 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg); IV solution
medicines.use_case: Long half-life BZD — used for alcohol detoxification; acute agitation; status epilepticus; IV diazepam for acute seizure management; oral tapering protocol for BZD dependence discontinuation

categories.category_name: Pregabalin and Gabapentin — For Refractory GAD and Social Anxiety

medicines.name: Pregabalin (Lyrica)
medicines.dosage: Start 25-50 mg twice daily; therapeutic dose for GAD: 150-300 mg/day in 2-3 divided doses; maximum 450-600 mg/day
medicines.use_case: GAD (particularly when somatic symptoms are prominent: muscle tension, physical anxiety symptoms); Social Anxiety Disorder; refractory anxiety not responding to SSRIs/SNRIs; particularly useful for patients with concurrent neuropathic pain or fibromyalgia; faster onset than SSRIs (1-2 weeks vs 4-8 weeks)
medicines.mechanism: Alpha-2-delta calcium channel subunit ligand — reduces excitatory neurotransmitter release from anxious neural circuits; reduces central sensitisation contributing to anxiety
medicines.abuse_potential: Some abuse potential noted (recreational euphoria at high doses); classify use carefully; not a Schedule H1 drug in India currently but prescribe with care in patients with substance use history

medicines.name: Propranolol
medicines.dosage: 10-40 mg taken 30-60 minutes before the anxiety-provoking situation (PRN — as needed); NOT for continuous daily use for anxiety disorders
medicines.use_case: SITUATIONAL / PERFORMANCE ANXIETY: examination anxiety (trembling, palpitations before JEE/NEET/interviews — propranolol reduces the peripheral physical symptoms; does not affect cognition; widely and legitimately used by medical students and professionals for pre-performance anxiety); stage fright; public speaking; driving test anxiety; NOT effective for generalised anxiety or panic disorder (does not cross blood-brain barrier sufficiently to address central anxiety mechanisms)
medicines.mechanism: Non-selective beta-adrenergic blocker — reduces sympathetically-mediated physical symptoms of anxiety (tachycardia, tremor, palpitations, sweating) without significantly altering central anxiety experience
medicines.contraindications: Asthma/COPD (bronchospasm risk); very important in India given high asthma prevalence; heart block; uncontrolled heart failure; diabetes (masks hypoglycaemia warning signs)

categories.category_name: Augmentation Strategies — When First-Line Treatments Fail

medicines.name: Mirtazapine — Augmentation for Insomnia and Anxiety
medicines.dosage: 7.5-15 mg at bedtime (sedating — uses low dose for insomnia); anxiety augmentation: 15-30 mg at night alongside SSRI/SNRI
medicines.use_case: Augmentation of SSRI for anxiety with significant insomnia; reduces SSRI-induced insomnia and sexual dysfunction; for anxiety with concurrent significant weight loss or poor appetite (mirtazapine increases appetite); unique mechanism (alpha-2 antagonist + 5-HT2A/3 antagonist) complements SSRI

medicines.name: Quetiapine (Low Dose) — Augmentation for Refractory GAD
medicines.form: Tablet (25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg, 150 mg extended-release)
medicines.dosage: 25-50 mg at bedtime for anxiety augmentation
medicines.use_case: Refractory GAD not responding to SSRIs, SNRIs, and buspirone; significant insomnia complicating anxiety; off-label but evidence-based for GAD augmentation; monitor weight and metabolic effects
medicines.note: Reserve for specialist use — low-dose quetiapine requires metabolic monitoring (glucose, lipids, weight)

medicines.name: Hydroxyzine
medicines.dosage: 25-50 mg three to four times daily
medicines.use_case: GAD; pruritus; relatively safe non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic with sedating properties; useful as short-term non-habit-forming anxiolytic; no abuse potential; available OTC in many Indian pharmacies

categories.purpose: Adjunctive treatments with emerging scientific evidence; deeply accepted in Indian traditional medical culture; should be discussed openly with patients who are likely using them regardless. NOT replacements for evidence-based treatments but potentially useful adjuncts.

medicines.name: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) — Adaptogen
medicines.dosage: 300-600 mg of standardised root extract (KSM-66 or Sensoril) once or twice daily
medicines.mechanism: Withanolides in ashwagandha modulate cortisol levels (adaptogenic — reduces cortisol spikes in response to stress); GABA receptor modulation; anti-inflammatory; anxiolytic in preclinical models; reduces thyroid-stimulating hormone (monitor thyroid in hypothyroid patients — may increase T4)
medicines.evidence: Multiple RCTs in India and globally: Chandrasekhar et al. (2012 — JACA, Indian trial): 300 mg KSM-66 twice daily significantly reduced anxiety (GAD-7), cortisol, and stress vs placebo over 60 days; Singh et al. (2015): 600 mg/day reduced anxiety and insomnia significantly; emerging evidence for chronic stress, GAD, and insomnia
medicines.safety: Generally well-tolerated; GI disturbance; thyroid effects (monitor TSH); possible interaction with sedatives and thyroid medications; AVOID in pregnancy
medicines.india_note: Ashwagandha is the most scientifically validated Ayurvedic anxiolytic; can be recommended as an evidence-based adjunct to CBT for mild-moderate anxiety in patients who prefer natural approaches or as culturally acceptable entry point into treatment

medicines.name: Brahmi (Bacopa monnieri) — Cognitive and Anxiolytic
medicines.evidence: RCTs show cognitive enhancement (memory, processing speed); anxiety reduction in chronic stress; GABA modulation and serotonergic activity; used in Ayurveda for 'medhya' (brain health) and anxious minds
medicines.use_case: Mild anxiety; cognitive complaints in anxiety; students with examination anxiety and memory concerns

medicines.name: Jatamansi (Nardostachys jatamansi) — Sedative Anxiolytic
medicines.use_case: Traditional Ayurvedic use for anxiety and insomnia; mild anxiolytic; available as herbal supplement; limited clinical trial evidence but long traditional use history in India

psychotherapy.overview: Psychotherapy — particularly Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) — is the most effective, evidence-based, and DURABLE treatment for anxiety disorders. Unlike medications (which reduce symptoms only while taken), psychotherapy teaches skills that persist after treatment ends, significantly reducing relapse rates. Every anxious patient deserves access to psychological treatment.

cbt_cognitive_behavioural_therapy.description: The gold standard psychological treatment for all anxiety disorders — with the largest and most robust evidence base of any psychological intervention for anxiety; more effective than medication alone in many studies; combination CBT + SSRI is most effective for moderate-severe anxiety
key_components: PSYCHOEDUCATION: understanding the CBT model of anxiety (thoughts → feelings → behaviours → physical symptoms); normalising anxiety; explaining the vicious cycle of anxiety and avoidance; the neuroscience of anxiety (amygdala hyperactivation, fight-or-flight response) — patients are relieved to understand their symptoms have a biological basis

COGNITIVE RESTRUCTURING: identifying and challenging anxious automatic thoughts; thought records; recognising cognitive distortions (catastrophising, probability overestimation, mind-reading, all-or-nothing thinking); developing balanced realistic counter-thoughts; evidence testing ('what is the realistic probability that the worst will happen?')

BEHAVIOURAL EXPERIMENTS: testing anxious predictions in real life; 'what will actually happen if I do X?' — designing small experiments to test fear predictions; discovering that feared outcomes usually don't occur (or are manageable if they do)

EXPOSURE THERAPY: the most powerful component — systematic, graduated approach to feared situations (from least to most feared); the goal is HABITUATION and INHIBITORY LEARNING (new learning that the feared situation is safe, overwriting the old fear association); the evidence-based principle: anxiety naturally habituates when maintained long enough without escape; avoidance prevents this natural learning

RELAXATION AND AROUSAL MANAGEMENT: controlled diaphragmatic breathing (the most evidence-based acute anxiety management technique); progressive muscle relaxation (PMR — systematically tensing and releasing muscle groups); applied relaxation (using relaxation as a coping skill in vivo, not just in the clinic)

MINDFULNESS INTEGRATION: in Mindfulness-Based CBT — developing an observer relationship with anxious thoughts; noticing thoughts without identifying with them ('I am having the thought that something bad will happen' vs 'something bad will happen')
cbt_cognitive_behavioural_therapy.number_of_sessions: Typically 8-16 weekly sessions (50-60 minutes each) for most anxiety disorders; some specific phobias respond to single session (3-hour intensive); panic disorder: 8-12 sessions; GAD: 12-16 sessions; social anxiety: 12-20 sessions (particularly if long-standing)
cbt_cognitive_behavioural_therapy.india_challenges: Severe shortage of trained CBT therapists in India (estimated 2,000 clinical psychologists for 1.4 billion people); concentrated in metro cities; cost (private CBT: Rs 1,500-5,000 per session — unaffordable for most); cultural factors (expressing feelings to a stranger is uncomfortable for many Indians; brief, solution-focused approaches may be culturally preferred over long-term therapy); SOLUTIONS: stepped care (low-intensity internet-delivered CBT first; face-to-face only for more severe); NIMHANS, TISS, and CMH institutions provide low-cost/free therapy; iCall (Tata Institute of Social Sciences) provides counselling; teletherapy/video CBT dramatically expanding access
